fatal_errors: The hypothesis assumes a transformative HCP epsilon phase, whereas the target coating and substrate are initially FCC and the relevant mediator is temperature-driven lattice disorder, stacking faults/HCP atom fraction, and dislocation-density evolution.
The proposed intervention changes unspecified alloying and processing variables rather than controlling temperature relative to the 300 K coating baseline.
It predicts improved wear resistance and reduced deformation, while the target behavior is stable performance through 600 K followed by sharply reduced hardness and wear resistance at 900–1200 K.
The baseline is an uncoated substrate rather than the same coating at room temperature, so the proposed comparison cannot identify the target thermal mechanism.
No quantitative temperature boundary is stated; the critical transition near 900 K is omitted.
The falsification test only assesses whether a coating outperforms an uncoated substrate and does not test whether epsilon-phase slip or twinning governs wear.
explanation: The response is aligned only at the broad level of a FeNiCrCoCu coating undergoing high-temperature sliding. Its central mechanism is imported from transformative HCP HEAs and does not reconstruct the target mechanism: relative stability at 300–600 K, an elastic-modulus maximum near 600 K associated with reduced dislocation density, and rapid disordering/softening above about 900 K accompanied by lower hardness and increased, strongly fluctuating friction. E2 supports c/a-dependent slip in epsilon martensite generally, but it does not establish that this phase or mechanism applies to the specified FCC FeNiCrCoCu/Cu coating. E1 is closer to the relevant alloy family but does not substantiate the claimed c/a mechanism. The experiment measures wear and deformation but neither isolates the claimed mediator nor distinguishes it from thermal softening, lattice disorder, or dislocation evolution.
